origins.name: Abdellah Zakibrug
origins.en: Abdellah Zaki (b. 1936 - Lelystad, 2017), was a Dutch-Moroccan artist with a love for history and culture. His work often focused on flowers and Amsterdam cityscapes. The name also symbolizes labor migration and the connection between two cultures.

origins.name: Ad Grimmonbrug
origins.en: Ad (Adriaan Alphonsus Maria) Grimmon (1883-1953 As a furniture maker, (interior) architect and color specialist, he developed from the craft tradition of the Amsterdam School to industrial modernism. His career covered the first half of the 20th century.

origins.name: Albert Helmanbrug
origins.en: Albert Helman is the pseudonym of Lodewijk Alphonsus Maria Lichtveld (1903-1996 He was a Dutch-Surinamese writer, politician and resistance fighter. His best-known novels are Zuid-Zuidwest from 1926 and De stille Plantage from 1931 He received an honorary doctorate from the University of Amsterdam and died in Buitenveldert.

origins.name: Aldo van Eyckbrug
origins.en: Aldo van Eyck (1918-1999) is best known as the architect of the Burgerweeshuis on the nearby IJsbaanpad. He was voted 'Dutch architect of the century' by his colleagues.

origins.name: Aluminiumbrug
origins.en: This lifting bridge is named so because in 1956 the fall (bridge deck) of this bridge (as the first in the Netherlands) was made of aluminum. Another name was Dwingerbrug, after the adjacent fortification 'Swijght Utrecht'.

origins.name: Amstelstroombrug
origins.en: The bridge is named after the lane. The Amstelstroomlaan is named after a former country house on the Amsteldijk, demolished in 1916. As early as 1583 there was a house here, which was known under the name Amstelstroom.

origins.name: Angenietje Swarthofbrug
origins.en: Around 1800, Amsterdam was dealing with thousands of orphans. The orphans came under the care of the Poor Children's Home on the Prinsengracht (near the bridge). They were housed with families in the city. These were women who wanted to supplement their family income with a widow's pension. Angenietje Swart is an example of this. She cared for a total of 126 children.

origins.name: Anna Paulownabrug
origins.en: Anna Paulowna (1795 - 1865) married the heir to the throne of Orange, the later king William II, on February 21, 1816. Through her marriage, she received the title of Princess Royal. After William I abdicated the throne on October 7, 1840, the inauguration of William II took place on November 28 in the Nieuwe Kerk in Amsterdam. Under Anna's influence, court life acquired more royal allure. Despite her, by her upbringing determined, distant and sometimes lofty attitude as queen, she was strongly involved in Dutch society. She had learned Dutch from court tutor Arie van der Spuij and mastered the language better than her husband, with whom she usually spoke French.

origins.name: Anna van Saksenbrug
origins.en: Named after Anna of Saxony (1544-1577), second wife of William of Orange and mother of Prince Maurice and Princess Anna.

origins.name: Annemie Wolffbrug
origins.en: The photographer Anna Maria Koller, known as Annemie Wolff, also known under the pseudonym Marianne (Germany 27-12-1906 - Amsterdam 2-2-1994), marries in Munich the architect and photographer Helmuth Egon Wilhelm Wolff (1895-1940). In May 1933 they flee to Amsterdam because Helmuth, as a Jew, can no longer work in Germany and there is an arrest warrant issued against him for false reasons. On the night of May 14 to 15, 1940, Annemie and Helmuth try to end their lives. They are found and transported to the Dutch Jewish Hospital where Helmuth dies. Annemie must get her life back on track as a young widow of 35 years old.

origins.name: Anton Jolingbrug
origins.en: Antonius Jacobus Joling (1857-1934), architect. Learned the trade from Pierre Cuypers (1827-1921), and began working for himself around 1887. Designed mainly public buildings such as offices, hospitals and schools. The building of Peek & Cloppenburg on the Dam is by Joling.

origins.name: Arlandabrug
origins.en: Name of Stockholm airport.

origins.name: Armand Sunierbrug
origins.en: Armand Louis Jean Sunier (Rotterdam, December 17, 1886 – Baarn, May 13, 1974) was a Dutch biologist and the third director of the Natura Artis Magistra zoo. Sunier prevented deportation of staff and animals to Germany and allowed blindfolded refugees to hide in the zoo. In addition, he was one of the most important people in the breeding program set up to prevent the wisent from becoming extinct. He was also a member for many years and in addition briefly president of the International Union of Directors of Zoological Gardens.

origins.name: Armbrug
origins.en: The seventh bridge over the Oudezijls Voorburgwal. The middle section of this wooden bridge in front of the O.Z. Armsteeg was removable, it was rebuilt in 1882 and renewed in 1906

origins.name: Aron Wolff Berlijnbrug
origins.en: Composer and conductor (1817-1870). Wrote more than two hundred works, including at least twenty major, romantic ballets for the Stadsschouwburg, where he was conductor from 1846.

origins.name: Baanbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Lijnbaansgracht, which was formerly called Baangracht

origins.name: Bantammerbrug
origins.en: The name of this permanent bridge evokes memories of the sixteenth century, when Dutchmen brought the products from Bantam (Dutch East Indies) to Amsterdam.

origins.name: Batavus Droogstoppelbrug
origins.en: Batavus Droogstoppel is a fictional character from Multatuli's Max Havelaar. He is a coffee broker at Lauriergracht 37. He is portrayed by Multatuli as an 'inferior product of dirty greed and blasphemous female prostitution'.

origins.name: Beemsterstraatbrug
origins.en: Name of underlying street

origins.name: Beltbrug
origins.en: Reminiscent of the municipal landfill, which served there until 1888.

origins.name: Berensluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after Berenstraat, to which it is adjacent. In the adjacent part of the current Jordaan, in the seventeenth century, the tanneries and the leather trade were located

origins.name: Berlagebrug
origins.en: Hendrik Petrus Berlage (1856-1934), architect. Chief architect of the Koopmansbeurs on the Damrak, among other things. Designer of the expansion plan-Zuid and the Mercatorplein and surroundings. His last creation was the Berlagebrug (1932). In 1966, Hildo Krop made a statue of him, which was placed on the Victorieplein.

origins.name: Berta de Vriesbrug
origins.en: Luberta de Hondt de Vries, known as Berta de Vries (Amsterdam 23-01-1885 - Amsterdam 19-04-1959), was active in the revolutionary-socialist women's movement, the Communist Party in the Netherlands and the Amsterdam Playground Association.

origins.name: Beudekerbrug
origins.en: Frans Beudeker (1815-1897) was director of the Stads-bestedelingenhuis for people who could not take care of themselves. 'He goes to Beudeker' was an expression in the nineteenth century for someone who was designated for care. The Stads-bestedelingenhuis was later converted into the Palace of Justice, which is located right next to this bridge.

origins.name: Blauwbrug
origins.en: The name of this permanent bridge recalls an earlier version of it, which was painted blue in the color of Nassau after the alteration of Amsterdam in 1578. The current bridge dates from 1884. The architects B. de Greef and W. Springer were inspired by a Seine Bridge. Another name for this bridge was Sophiabrug, despite all changes the name Blauwbrug was maintained. This was once another name, for the Blauwbrug, which was never adopted, just like Sophiaplein in front of Muntplein. Sophia of Württemberg (1817-1877) was the first wife of King William III, who opened this renovated bridge in 1839.

origins.name: Boerenweteringbrug
origins.en: The name of the water, which originally ran from Kalfjeslaan to the current Koningsplein. Also formerly called Oude Wetering, in contrast to the Nieuwe Wetering (Kostverlorenvaart). The Weteringbuurt and the Weteringschans derive their name from this water.

origins.name: Boy Edgarbrug
origins.en: George Willem Fred (Boy) Edgar (1915-1980), composer and arranger of entertainment music, originally a doctor. With his compositions, he contributed greatly to the repertoire of light music.

origins.name: Buiksloterdraaibrug
origins.en: The Buikslotermeerpolder, a lake drained in 1628.

origins.name: Bullebak
origins.en: The bull's head was a mythical water ghost, which not only roamed around the old sluice gate near the Haarlemmerplein, but also under the stone vault that connected the Bloemgracht with the Buitensingel (bridge 160). According to tradition, the monster lay there waiting to pull passersby who dared to venture too close to the water into the water.

origins.name: Camera Obscurabrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the book Camera Obscura, which was published in 1839 by Hildebrand, a pseudonym of Nicolaas Beets (1814-1903).

origins.name: Caroline Herschelbrug
origins.en: Caroline Herschel (Hannover, 1750 – Hanover, 1848) was involved in the construction and grinding of lenses of the largest telescopes of the 17th century and she discovered and described previously unobserved nebulae. In addition, Caroline Herschel made many independent observations. She was the first woman with a paid scientific position.

origins.name: Cecilia van Alphen-Jagtmanbrug
origins.en: Cecilia Maria Cornelia Jagtman (1910-1972) was an action member of the CPN with her husband Pieter van Alphen (1909-1953) and during World War II, with danger to her own life, she produced and distributed, among other things, the illegal newspaper De Waarheid. He was arrested by the Nazis in April 1941. She continued the activities. She also hid refugees in her house at Fresiastraat 12 in Amsterdam-North.

origins.name: Ceintuurbrug
origins.en: At the end of the nineteenth century, a beltway or belt was laid around a large part of the city, which later took the name Ceintuurbaan as far as this road was between the Boerenwetering and the Amstel. The other parts later received other names, because a middle section was not yet in Amsterdam at that time.

origins.name: Charley Tooropbrug
origins.en: Charley Toorop (1891-1955) developed her own style, the Expressive Business Realism. She is generally considered the most powerful woman in Dutch painting of the twentieth century

origins.name: Corry Tendeloobrug
origins.en: Nancy Sophie Cornélie Tendeloo (1897-1956), politician, feminist and advocate. Municipal council member for the Free Democratic Union (VDB) from 1938-1941, and from 1945-1956 VDB and PvdA parliamentary member. Among other things, in 1955 she tabled a motion to abolish the dismissal of married women from government service, which happened a year later.

origins.name: Dageraadsbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the former, nearby shipyard 'De Dageraad'.

origins.name: De Duifbrug
origins.en: Named after the church De Duif at Prinsengracht 754, which is officially called Sint Willibrordus within the Veste.

origins.name: Dick Schmüllbrug
origins.en: Diederich Herman 'Dick' Schmüll (Sumatra, 1908 - Amsterdam, 1990) is the founder of the Dutch Basketball Federation and the Dutch Volleyball Federation.

origins.name: Dirk de Waterduikerbrug
origins.en: Dirk Rietveldt (1858-1940) saved many people (perhaps 74), dogs and cats from the water of the Amsterdam canals. He was therefore a very respected figure in

origins.name: Doelensluis
origins.en: This permanent bridge owes its name to the Kloveniersdoelen. The targets were places where the shooting guilds gathered and where they practiced shooting at a target. These targets had their seat at the Svych Utrecht tower (on the site of the current Doelenhotel). They practiced on the grounds of the Old Nonnenklooster (grounds Binnengasthuis).

origins.name: Dr. Samuel de Ranitzbrug
origins.en: Doctor (1834-1913). Practiced in Amsterdam from 1861. Affected by the miserable conditions in which many sick Amsterdam children were living, he decided in 1865 to establish the later Emma Children's Hospital. In 1873, the institution moved to Sarphatistraat, not far from the location of this bridge, where it remained for 117 years.

origins.name: Drieharingenbrug
origins.en: This pickup bridge gets its name from the three hake above the door of the house 'De Drie Haringen' in Vierwindendwarsstraat no.1.

origins.name: Drs. P-brug
origins.en: Drs. P (Thun, August 24, 1919 – Amsterdam, June 13, 2015), pseudonym of Heinz Hermann Polzer, was a Dutch-speaking lyricist with Swiss nationality. His stage name, devised by Willem Duys, refers to the academic degree of doctorandus (abbreviated: drs.) in economics, which Polzer obtained from the Dutch Economic University (now Erasmus University). He was also a poet, writer, cabaret performer, literary scholar, composer, pianist and singer of his own songs.

origins.name: Duizendste Brug
origins.en: On April 2, 1974, this bridge was opened as the thousandth bridge in Amsterdam by alderman Han Lammers

origins.name: Elsje Christiaensbrug
origins.en: Elsje Christiaens is an 18-year-old Danish girl who was strangled on the Dam in 1664 because she had murdered her mistress with an axe. She was hanged on the gallows.

origins.name: Enneüs Heermabrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after Enneüs Heerma (1944-1999).

origins.name: Etty Hillesumbrug
origins.en: Etty Hillesum (Middelburg, 15-01-1914 – Auschwitz approx. 30-11-1943) is a Jewish writer who wrote her diaries in the first years of World War II.

origins.name: Eva Schalkbrug
origins.en: Eva Schalk (1890-1978) was the first woman on a water board. She was the head country of the polder Buik Slotermeer for 27 years and the head country of the High Authority for Waters for 21 years.

origins.name: Ezelsbrug
origins.en: The name of this bridge recalls the difficult struggle that the residents had to fight against the car lobby, which preferred to see bridges for normal traffic realized here. They often felt like donkeys who had to bump into the same stone over and over again. The name is also a reference to the tool, which is called the donkey bridge. The bridge was officially opened on March 14, 1987 by letting a donkey walk over it.

origins.name: Fré Cohenbrug
origins.en: Frederika Sophia Cohen (1903-1943), graphic artist, who gave shape to design in the 1930s with her brochures, covers, book bindings and other work. Worked from 1929-1941 for the Stadsdrukkerij Amsterdam. Added her own twist to influences from Jugendstil, Amsterdam School and De Stijl. Continued working during the underground period until she was betrayed.

origins.name: Galgenbrug
origins.en: The name refers to the view from this bridge of the gallows of the Volewijk, which stood here until 1795

origins.name: Geert Geertsenbrug
origins.en: Geert Geertsen is the birth name of Desiderius Erasmus (1467-1536). Because his Dutch name is related to the word desire, he took the Latin word for desire as his first name and the Greek word as his last name.

origins.name: George Madurobrug
origins.en: George John Lionel Maduro (1916-1945) was a resistance fighter of Antillean origin who died in the Dachau concentration camp. The miniature city of Madurodam in The Hague is named after him.

origins.name: Ger van Zanenbrug
origins.en: Ger van Zanen (1929-2015) was a passionate nature lover and from 1960 until his death a member of the Royal Dutch Natural History Society Amsterdam (KNNV). Under the leadership of Ger van Zanen, many field biological studies and inventories were carried out in Amsterdam. Ger van Zanen was always willing to guide anyone interested in nature. The bridge leads from the residential area to the Ruige Riet, a valuable and still untouched nature reserve, part of the Sloterpark. This area is rich in mushrooms, among other things, and participants in mushroom excursions often walk across the bridge and will all remember Ger van Zanen.

origins.name: Gerda Tarobrug
origins.en: Gerda Taro (1910-1937) was the first female photographer on the front lines. She fought against Nazism and given her activism, she has grown into a symbol of antifascism.

origins.name: Gerrie Mührenbrug
origins.en: Gerrie (Gerrit) Mühren

origins.name: Gierzwaluwbrug
origins.en: The swallow (Apus apus) is a very special bird. Swallows spend almost their entire lives in the air. They eat, drink, mate and even sleep while flying! They only land in the spring on a fixed nesting site, usually under roof tiles. They breed in almost all cities in Europe, also in the center of Amsterdam. While flying, they mainly catch mosquitoes. They are extremely fast and agile in the air, but after landing on the nest they can only slide on their short legs.

origins.name: Goudvinkbrug
origins.en: The goldfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) is perhaps the most beautiful bird in our country. Both males and females have a black head. The male can be recognized by its bright rosy belly and cheeks. Goldfinches can be found in this park all year round, but despite the bright colors difficult to see. Many inconspicuous brown birds can sing beautifully, but this beautiful bird can only make squeaky sounds. You can't have everything, either. In the Bijlmerweide near the G-district, seven bridges have been given bird names that start with a G. Urban ecologists gave a workshop on birds to children from the local Kidsclub, after which they chose their favorite bird species.

origins.name: Grimnessesluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Grim (muddy ditch) water, which formed the southern boundary of the city from 1342 until around 1400.

origins.name: Groene spechtbrug
origins.en: The green woodpecker (Picus viridis) cuts a hole in the tree to make a nest. Cutting it out takes more than two weeks, so they often use an already existing cavity. Groene woodpeckers have a very long, sticky tongue with which they can suck insects behind the tree bark. But they mainly eat ants, on the ground. You can easily recognize them by their moss green back and the red cap on their head. A fun fact: they can also laugh very loudly! In the Bijlmerweide near the G-district, seven bridges have been given bird names that start with a G. Urban ecologists gave a workshop on birds to children from the local Kidsclub, after which they chose their favorite bird species.

origins.name: Groentemarktbrug
origins.en: Named after the vegetable market that was held here in the neighborhood until 1934. In that year, trade was moved to the Central Market Halls.

origins.name: Groentepraambrug
origins.en: The name of this bridge reminds us of the time when many vegetable carts carried vegetables from the west via the Admiralengrachten to the Kostverlorenkade to the Marnixstraat, where the vegetables were traded. Carts are low boats that can easily pass through polder locks and under footbridges.

origins.name: Gwijde van Henegouwenbrug
origins.en: Also known as: Guy van Avesnes or Gui d'Avesnes (1253-1317). Bishop of Utrecht. Was personal administrator of the possessions of the Lords of Amstel. Just before his consecration in Utrecht, he granted Amsterdam city privileges in 1300 or 1301.

origins.name: Haardsteebrug
origins.en: Name of a farm near Steenderen (Gelderland).

origins.name: Haarlemmersluis
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Haarlemmerstraat, which is the main road from Amsterdam to Haarlem

origins.name: Halvemaansbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge derives its name from Halvemaansteeg. The origin of this name may be found on the facade of Halvemaanssteeg No. 18, with the indication 'Van Ouds de Halve Maan'

origins.name: Han Lammersbrug
origins.en: Han Lammers (1931 - 2000) worked as a journalist for the ANP, the Algemeen Dagblad and De Groene Amsterdammer, before becoming a member of the municipal council and alderman for the PvdA in the municipality of Amsterdam in 1970. In 1965, he was involved in the founding of the renewal movement Nieuw Links, among other things, together with Jan Nagel. As a councillor for urban development, Lammers gave the first impetus to urban renewal. He had plans drawn up for the demolition of entire residential areas, from the Jordaan to the Dapperbuurt completely new residential areas would be built from the ground up, with a completely different street plan.

origins.name: Han van Zomerenbrug
origins.en: Han van Zomeren (1920-1941) was a graphic designer and active in the resistance during the German occupation. He printed pamphlets calling for resistance. He was executed on the Larense Heide in 1941 and reburied in 1952 at the Erebegraafplaats in Overveen.

origins.name: Hannie Schaftbrug
origins.en: Hannie Schaft (1920-1945) was a Haarlem communist and resistance fighter. She is known as the Girl with the Red Hair. She carried out several attacks on Germans and collaborators and was therefore shot dead by the Germans herself on April 17, 1945 in the dunes near Bloemendaal. On November 27, 1945, her body was reburied at the Bloemendaal Memorial Cemetery in Overveen.

origins.name: Hanny Michaelisbrug
origins.en: Hanny Michaelis (Amsterdam 19-12-1922 − Amsterdam 11-6-2007) was a poet, writer and translator. She debuted in 1949 with Klein voorspel. Until 1971, five other poetry collections with new work were published. In addition, she wrote (autobiographical) prose and made a number of translations.

origins.name: Hans Kressebrug
origins.en: Hans Kresse was an important comic book artist and a native Amsterdammer. He became known for his graphic novels of Eric de Noorman. Kresse has created many history-based comics and stories, which have become world famous.

origins.name: Haringpakkersbrug
origins.en: While in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the herring sellers often lived on the Nieuwendijk, these and other alleys along that dike were the homes of the herring packers. For the old Haringpakkerij, see Prins Hendrikkade. The alley was called Kapelsteeg until 1913, but was then renamed because of confusion with the other Kapelstegen in Haringpakkerssteeg.

origins.name: Hartmanbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after cigar shop owner André Hartman, who died on November 6, 1993 in a robbery of his store. The bridge is also a tribute to his wife An Hartman and to all shopkeepers who work under dangerous circumstances.

origins.name: Heibrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Heisteeg, to which it is located. The Heisteeg derives its name from a corner house that was called 't Hayblok. This house is already mentioned at the beginning of the sixteenth century. An unofficial name for this bridge was Strontenburgerbrug until 1606. It was named so because of the environmental nuisance, caused by two nearby shipyards.

origins.name: Hein Donnerbrug
origins.en: Jan Hein Donner (1927-1988) was a chess grandmaster, who became champion of the Netherlands several times. He was also a polemicist and columnist for the NRC-Handelsblad.

origins.name: Hennetjesbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge was probably once a narrow wooden chicken bridge

origins.name: Henrietta Leavittbrug
origins.en: Henrietta Swan Leavitt (1868-1921), American astronomer. Discovered a relationship between the brightness and the period of pulsation of certain stars. Thanks to her discovery, astronomers were able to calculate the distance between distant star systems and the earth for the first time. Her work also laid the foundation for calculating the expanding universe.

origins.name: Henriëtte van Heukelom-van den Brandelerbrug
origins.en: Hendrika Jacoba van den Brandeler-Heukelom (1884-1985), composer and pianist. Student of Dirk Schäfer (1873-1931), among others. She wrote songs, a requiem for her father and a Stabat Mater, which was performed in 1913 by the Concertgebouw Orchestra.

origins.name: Horst Blankenburgbrug
origins.en: Horst Blankenburg born July 10, 1947 in Heidenheim an der Brenz (Germany) 2 x National Champion / 2 x winner KNVB Cup / 3 x winner Europa Cup National Champions / 2 x winner European Supercup / 1 x winner World Cup, Played 188 competitive matches for Ajax. In 1969, Ajax reached the final in the prestigious Europa Cup for National Champions as the first Dutch club. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize. In the following two years, Ajax extended the title and thus confirmed itself as the flag bearer of Dutch football.

origins.name: Hortusbrug
origins.en: To the opposite Hortus Botanicus.

origins.name: Hugo de Vriesbrug
origins.en: Botanist (1848-1935), professor at the University of Amsterdam 1880-1918. He developed the mutation theory, which assumes sudden change of characteristics. The theory applies to all living organisms, so not only to plants.

origins.name: Huntumbrug
origins.en: Patrician house on the Vecht, south of Vreeland.

origins.name: Ina Boekbinderbrug
origins.en: Ina Boekbinder (Assen, 1915 – Hilversum, 1987) was a Jewish resistance fighter during World War II. She helped Jewish children hide and distributed food coupons to the underground. In addition, she carried stethoscopes in her bicycle bags and robbed a medical supply depot.

origins.name: Isa van Eeghenbrug
origins.en: Isabelle Henriette van Eeghen (1913-1996), archivist and historian. Produced many pieces between 1944-1978 at the City Archive, near this bridge, including a voluminous work on Amsterdam bookstores. Organized the purchase of Jacob Olie's photo collection (1834-1905). Member of the Genootschap Amstelodamum. Received the Silver Pen in 1971.

origins.name: Isaac Israëlsbrug
origins.en: Isaac Israels (1865-1934) was the son of Joseph Israels (1824-1911) and also a painter. He was a representative of the Amsterdam School in painting together with George Breitner, Willem Witsen, Jac. van Looy and Jan Eduard Karsen. He painted factory girls and city impressions, among other things. During the 1928 Olympic Games in Amsterdam, he won a gold Olympic art medal in the category Painting for his painting 'The Red Rider This bridge connects to Breitnerstraat and is close to Willem Witsenstraat.

origins.name: Jacoba van Tongerenbrug
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1903-1967). As a social worker, she was involved in illegal activities such as courier work, and then founded Group 2000, a 140-member organization that helped up to 4500 refugees. Was nicknamed 'The Queen of the Stamps' thanks to her stamp smuggling using a special vest. Received the Yad Vashem award in 1990.

origins.name: Jan Evertsenbrug
origins.en: Johan Evertsen (1600-1666), belonging to a Zeelandish family of sea heroes. Participated as an admiral in several naval battles, including the Battle of Duins (1639). Killed in the Second English War.

origins.name: Jan Schaeferbrug
origins.en: Johannes Lodewijk Nicolaas Schaefer (1940-1994), politician for the Labour Party. He was a member of the House of Representatives from 1971, was state secretary for urban renewal at the Ministry of Housing and Spatial Planning in the Den Uyl Cabinet from 1973 to 1977, and was a city councillor (housing affairs, urban renewal, building and housing supervision, land management) in Amsterdam from 1978 to 1986. From him come the winged words: "You can't live in nonsense." Provided a huge impetus to urban renewal and housing production in Amsterdam.

origins.name: Jan Swammerdambrug
origins.en: Jan Swammerdam (1637-1680), anatomist and physicist. Conducted important microscopic research, preserved in his 'Bible of Nature'.

origins.name: Jan Wilsbrug
origins.en: is named after Jan Wils (1891-1972). He was the architect of the Olympic Stadium and the two Citroën buildings on Stadionplein. He also designed the Citytheater on Kleine-Gartmanplantsoen

origins.name: Joep Langebrug
origins.en: Joep Lange was a professor of infectious diseases and AIDS specialist. He was one of the most influential AIDS scientists in the world. He died on July 17, 2014 in the MH17 plane crash.

origins.name: Joes Kloppenburgbrug
origins.en: Joes Kloppenburg (1970- 1996) was killed on August 17, 1996 by Richard L., when he intervened in a street fight in the Voetboogsteeg with the words 'Cut it out!'. This bridge is relatively close to the place where he died and is intended as a symbol against senseless violence.

origins.name: Johan Cruijffbrug
origins.en: Johan Cruijff born April 25, 1947 in Amsterdam / died March 24, 2016 in Barcelona. Striker Ajax 1964-1973

origins.name: Johan Neeskensbrug
origins.en: Johan Neeskens born September 15, 1951 in Heemstede, Ajax 1970 - 1974 124 matches in Eredivisie. Midfielder 3x national champion of the Netherlands/ 3 x winner KNVB Cup / 3 x winner Europa Cup National Champions / 1 x winner Europa Cup Cup Winners / 1 x winner World Cup / 2 x winner European Supercup, 49 x international, played two World Cup finals. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final in the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Johanna Borskibrug
origins.en: Johanna Borski (1764-1846) was called 'the financier of the Netherlands', because she invested in visionary projects such as De Nederlandsche Bank, De Nederlandsche Handelsmaatschapperij and the Hollandsche IJzeren Spoorweg Maatschappij. She saved the Dutch state from bankruptcy twice. She was born as Johanna van der Velde in the Vijzelstraat and had an office on the Keizersgracht near the Spiegelstraat. This bridge offers views of the building of the Nederlandsche Handelsmaatschappij, which she helped establish and which she saved from destruction twice.

origins.name: John Rädeckerbrug
origins.en: John Rädecker (1885-1956, born and died in Amsterdam) drew, painted, made graphic work, wooden sculptures and processed wood. Rädecker made his first sculptures from brick, such as the Worker, for De Dageraad in Amsterdam. John Rädecker became best known as a designer of sculptures on the National Monument on the Dam

origins.name: Johnny & Jonesbrug
origins.en: Johnny & Jones is the name of an Amsterdam jazz duo. In it, Nol van Wesel (1918-1945) was Johnny and Max Kannewasser (1916-1945) Jones. They were Jewish and were therefore interned in the transit camp Westerbork in 1943. Nevertheless, they managed to return to Amsterdam for a short time for some record sessions, including the 'Westerbork Serenade'. On September 4, they were transported to Germany, where they eventually died of exhaustion just before the liberation of the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp. Their most famous song was 'Mr. Dinges, I don't know what swing is'.

origins.name: Kabouterbrug
origins.en: The Kabouterbrug is named after the Gnome Movement (period 1969-1974), a playful protest movement and local political party.

origins.name: Kadoelenbrug
origins.en: Name for the part of the municipality of Landsmeer that was annexed to Amsterdam on August 1, 1966. The name Kadoelen (or Quadolen) already appears in 1375. In 1429, there is talk of the lordship of Landsmeer and the lordship of Quadolen, which then had one lord together. Old maps indicate Kadoelen as a hamlet along the Waterlandse zeedijk (Landsmeerderdijk). The Kadoelenweg was taken over on 1-8-1966 under the name Zuideinde, but in 1970 that name was changed due to confusion with the Zuideinde (former Oostzaan).

origins.name: Kattenburgerbrug
origins.en: One of the three eastern islands, next to Wittenburg and Oostenburg. is already referred to by the name Kattenburg for the paving and construction in the second half of the seventeenth century. A reason for this name has not been found to date. However, there was a house with the name 'de Cat', but that name is only mentioned in the eighteenth century. After many buildings had already been demolished during the occupation years, the rest was demolished in the years 1965 to 1968. After that, construction began again according to a new street pattern. Kattenburgerplein is the only one that still reminds you of the old buildings.

origins.name: Kattenslootbrug
origins.en: Name of underlying ditch

origins.name: Kees Fensbrug
origins.en: Kees Fens (1929 -2008) was an Amsterdam literary critic, essayist and literary scholar. In 1990 he received the P.C. Hooft Prize and in 2004 he received an honorary doctorate from the University of Amsterdam. From his house he had a view of this bridge and in 2008 he published the book 'The happiness of the bridge'.

origins.name: Keizersbrug
origins.en: It derives its name from the nearby Keizersstraat

origins.name: Kinkerbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after Johannes Kinker (1765-1845), poet and lawyer in Amsterdam and The Hague. After that, he became a professor in Liège.

origins.name: Klimopbrug
origins.en: Named after the ivy, a climbing shrub.

origins.name: Koekjesbrug
origins.en: There are four possible explanations for the name of this permanent bridge. It may have been named after a popular cookie seller, who fell into the mud here due to intrusive boys. There used to be a cocoa mill here as well, where cookies made from cocoa were sold. It is also possible that the name dates back to gardener Pannenkoek, who used to own land next to this bridge. A fourth possibility is that it is named after agent Koek, who walked demonstratively across this bridge shortly before the opening of this bridge after an argument with the ferry boss. After this, the ferry boss would have written on the bridge railing 'This bridge has been named Koekjesbrug'.

origins.name: Kors van Bennekombrug
origins.en: Kors van Bennekom (Lodewijk, July 13, 1933 – Amsterdam, October 4, 2016) was an Amsterdam photographer and was the holder of the Frans Banninck Cocqpenning of the Municipality of Amsterdam.

origins.name: Korte Ouderkerkerbrug
origins.en: Named after the village of Ouderkerk aan de Amstel, where these roads lead to it. The addition Korte dates from 1956, after the dike was dug through for the industrial area.

origins.name: Krijtbergbrug
origins.en: Named after the neighboring Krijtberg or Sint Franciscus Xavieruskerk (sometimes also called Rijtjeskerk) on the Singel. This church, inaugurated in 1883, took over the place of the former chapel in the house de Crijtberg, which was served by the Jesuits.

origins.name: L.H. Sarlouisbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after Louis Hartog Sarlouis (1884-1942). He was the founder of the Jewish H.B.S. and chief rabbi in Amsterdam from 1936 to 1942, in which year he was deported to Auschwitz, where he died

origins.name: Lau Mazirelbrug
origins.en: Laura Carola Mazirel (1907-1974), lawyer and prosecutor in Amsterdam. She campaigned for groups of people who were isolated in society. Before World War II, these were German refugees, after the war gypsies and homosexuals. During World War II, she was involved in both the children's daycare center of the Hollandse Schouwburg, where the Jewish population was concentrated for their deportation, and the resistance group around Gerrit van der Veen.

origins.name: Lee Millerbrug
origins.en: Lee Miller (1907-1977) was an American photographer and fashion model. She is known as a war correspondent during World War II. Lee Miller further developed herself into a renowned fashion and art photographer.

origins.name: Leeuwenputbrug
origins.en: In the first half of the 17th century, the gallows field was embellished with a stone well with three high columns with lion heads, as if it were a solemn ceremony taking place there. The body parts fell into the well over time. When the IJ froze in winter, which still happened regularly at the time, people would skate or sled across the ice to take a look. The ice entertainment around the gallows pit could take bizarre forms, as can be seen on a drawing by Reinier Vinkeles from around 1780. Near the pit are two pie and soup stalls with busy customers. A man urinates against the pit to apparently demonstrate his disgust.

origins.name: Leidsebrug
origins.en: The city of Leiden.

origins.name: Lex van Deldenbrug
origins.en: Alexander Zwaap (1919-1988), composer. Van Delden was the name he used from his time as a fugitive and resistance fighter. He received the Medal of Merit of the City of Amsterdam in 1982.

origins.name: Liefdesbruggetje
origins.en: This bridge is called Liefdesbruggetje, because it is a favorite place for taking wedding photos. You can look out over the park and the pond from here without seeing the buildings.

origins.name: Lijnbaansbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Lijnbaanssteeg, in which it lies. This alley dates back to the fifteenth century, when the Singel was the outer canal and the lineways of the rope-making works were located here on a kind of industrial site.

origins.name: Lyceumbrug
origins.en: The name of this bridge refers to the nearby Amsterdam Lyceum

origins.name: M. Justbrug
origins.en: Named after Chief Rabbi Meir Just (1908-2010), who worked in Buitenveldert. He lived in Soetendael and therefore often walked across this bridge to the Jewish Cultural Center on Van der Boechorststraat

origins.name: M.S. Vaz Diasbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after Moses Salomon Vaz Dias (1882-1963), founder of the M.S. Vaz Dias Press Agency, which merged in 1934 into the General Dutch Press Agency (ANP), which he co-founded.

origins.name: Machineslootbrug
origins.en: This bridge keeps the memory alive of one of the former names of the current Admiralengracht

origins.name: Madibabrug
origins.en: Nickname of Nelson Mandela

origins.name: Magere Brug
origins.en: Around 1670, a drawbridge was built over the Amstel, which was so narrow that it was only suitable for pedestrians. Although this bridge was officially called Kerkstraatbrug (after Lange Kerkstraat), it was stubbornly called 'Magere bridge' in popular parlance. Then this name was taken over by the municipal government. The story about the ladies Mager, who lived there nearby, belongs to the realm of legends. From old images it can be seen that the old bridge was a simple wooden construction, the deck of the fixed part was laid on simple wooden beams, while the movable middle part was formed by a 1-fold lifting bridge.

origins.name: Majoor Bosshardtbrug
origins.en: Alida Margaretha Bosshardt (1913-2007) became known for her work for the Salvation Army, which took place largely in the immediate vicinity of this bridge. She also founded the Goodwill Center here in the Wallows. In 2009, she was elected as the 'Greatest Amsterdammer of all time'. The 'major' (who was actually a lieutenant colonel) was a real bridge builder between various groups and that is why a bridge name naming was preferred over a street name naming

origins.name: Margaret Bourke-Whitebrug
origins.en: Margaret Bourke-White (1904-1971) was the first war correspondent of the U.S. Army and photographer of the U.S. Air Force.

origins.name: Mariniersbrug
origins.en: To the nearby Marine Barracks.

origins.name: Marten Toonderbrug
origins.en: Marten Toonder (Rotterdam, May 2, 1912 – Laren, July 27, 2005) was a Dutch comic book writer. In addition to his great role in literature, Toonder also used his talents during World War II.

origins.name: Meerbrug
origins.en: The name of this permanent bridge in Kadoelen is derived from the surrounding hamlet called 't Meertje, which belonged to Landsmeer before the annexation of 1921.

origins.name: Mien Ruysbrug
origins.en: Wilhelmina Jacoba (Mien) Moussault-Ruys, better known by her maiden name as Mien Ruys (Dedemsvaart, April 12, 1904 - Deventer, January 9, 1999), was an internationally known Dutch garden architect. In the Netherlands, she was nicknamed Bielzen Mien because she was the pioneer in the use of railway bogies in gardens, something that was particularly popular in the 1970s. She liked to work with straight shapes: rectangles, squares and clear lines. She was one of the first in the Netherlands to seriously deal with smaller city gardens as a garden architect.

origins.name: Muiderbergbrug
origins.en: To the town of Muiderberg

origins.name: Muntsluis
origins.en: The Amsterdammers simply call it the Mint. In the building next to the Mint Tower (remnant of the Regulierspoort), coins were minted for a period of time in the seventeenth century. Since then, the name Mint has been associated with it.

origins.name: Nesciobrug
origins.en: Nescio was the pseudonym of the Amsterdam writer J.H.F. Grönloh, known for novellas such as De Uitvreter and Titaantjes. He enjoyed walking in the area around the neighboring Diemerzeedijk and the Buiten-IJ.

origins.name: Nieuwe Amstelbrug
origins.en: At the delivery in 1903 of this, partly designed by Berlage, double bascule bridge, this was the latest bridge over the Amstel. The High Lock was also known as the Amstel Bridge, but this bridge was newer, hence the Nieuwe Amstelbrug

origins.name: Nieuwe-Wercksbrug
origins.en: Named after the original name for the current Jordaan.

origins.name: NSM-brug
origins.en: refers to the Nederlandsche Scheepsbouw Maatschappij, which was here until 1946. After merging with the NSM, it continued as NDSM with the Nederderlandsche Dok Maatschappij (NDM).

origins.name: Oetewalerbrug
origins.en: bridge from 1924 is named after the village of Oetewaal, or Outewaal or Houtewaal, which used to be located on the Zeedijk near the current Muiderpoort. The village, which was already mentioned in 1387, was burned down by the Spanish in 1575 and devastated by a storm surge in 1651, but rebuilt again and again. In 1658 it was annexed by the municipality of Amsterdam. Linnaeusstraat was called Oetewalerweg before 1878 and was the road from Oetewaal to Watergraafsmeer De Oetewalerbrug is also popularly known as Hemabrug due to the proximity of the Hema

origins.name: Omvalbrug
origins.en: Landtong between the Amstel and the ring canal of the Watergraafsmeer. Since the seventeenth century or earlier so named after a 'wreck' located there, that is, a construction site or ruin. The name has been passed down with the transition on 1-1-1921 of this part of the municipality of Ouder-Amstel.

origins.name: Oost-Indische Huisbrug
origins.en: Named after the nearby Oost-Indische House on the Kloveniersburgwal corner of Oude Hoogstraat

origins.name: Oosterbeerbrug
origins.en: Oosterbeer is a former stronghold, on which the De Gooyer mill stood for a while.

origins.name: Osdorperwegbrug
origins.en: To the neighborhood of Osdorp. On old maps, this neighborhood is mentioned as Oostdorp. In 1957, construction began on the garden city of Osdorp, which was practically completed in 1973. The Osdorperweg used to bear the names Herenstraat (in the village of Sloten) and Slimmeweg.

origins.name: Oude Haagsebrug
origins.en: This bridge, which is currently in use as a bus lane, is named after the road it lies on. This road used to lead to The Hague as part of the former Rijksweg 4. Now that this has not been the case since 1966, this road is called the Oude Haagsweg.

origins.name: Oude Kinkerbrug
origins.en: Johannes Kinker (1764-1845) was a Dutch poet, philosopher and lawyer

origins.name: Overschiebrug-Noord
origins.en: The former village in South Holland, part of Rotterdam since 1941.

origins.name: Overschiebrug-Zuid
origins.en: The former village in Zuid-Holland, since 1941 part of Rotterdam.

origins.name: Paleis voor Volksvlijtbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Paleis for Volksvlijt, which was burned down in 1929 and stood where the current Nederlandsche Bank is located.

origins.name: Pastoorsbrug
origins.en: The derivation of the name of this permanent bridge is not known with certainty. Perhaps the former Roman Catholic secret church 'De Zaaier', which was located at Keizersgracht 22, has something to do with this bridge name.

origins.name: Pelikaanbrug
origins.en: Given the proximity of the d'Peliekaan warehouse at Hoogte Kadijk 51

origins.name: Peter Postbrug
origins.en: Peter Post (1933-2011) In 1949, this Amsterdam native won his first cycling championship at the Amsterdam Slagersjongens and then he would grow up as a track cyclist to become the undisputed 'Emperor of the Six Days'. As a road cyclist, he won Paris-Roubaix in 1964. As team manager, he led Joop Zoetemelk to the final victory in the Tour de France in 1980.

origins.name: Pia Beckbrug
origins.en: Pieternella (Pia) Beck (1926 - 2009) was a Dutch jazz pianist. She was named the best jazz pianist in the world by her colleague Oscar Peterson. She was one of the first artists to openly come out as lesbian. In the Park Haagseweg, all the streets are named after famous jazz musicians.

origins.name: Piet Bakkerbrug
origins.en: Piet Bakker was a writer and journalist. In addition to his love for the Pijp, Piet Bakker also expressed his love for Amsterdam in books such as 'Amsterdam as it lives and works' from 1933 and 'Guide to Amsterdam' from 1937. But he has given Amsterdam above all its most iconic 'darling' in the person of Ciske de Rat, to whom two successful films and a musical are dedicated. In the vicinity

origins.name: Piet Keizerbrug
origins.en: Piet Keizer born June 14, 1943 in Amsterdam / died February 10, 2017 in Amsterdam. Striker Ajax 1961 - 1974 365 matches in Eredivisie (146 goals) 6 x national champion / 5 winner x KNVB Cup / 3 x winner European Cup for national champions / 2 x winner European Supercup/ 1 x winner Intertoto cup / 1 winner world cup. Piet Keizer played 34 international matches and never played for a club other than Ajax. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final of the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final, but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Piet Meerburgbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after Piet Meerburg, who was born in De Bilt in 1919 and died in Amsterdam in 2010. He was involved in saving Jewish children during World War II, for which he received the Yad Vashem award. One of those children was the later mayor Ed van Thijn. He was also a prominent theater entrepreneur in Amsterdam. For example, he was director of the Nieuwe de la Mar theater for many years and produced the musical My Fair Lady.

origins.name: Pieter Goemansbrug
origins.en: Pieter Goemans (Peter Shott), who lived from 1925 to 2000 in the 1950s, found inspiration for his song 'Aan de Amsterdamse grachten' on this fixed bridge. A plaque on this bridge reminds us of this.

origins.name: Raampoort
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Raampoort, which was demolished in 1844

origins.name: Reesluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Reestraat, in which it lies.

origins.name: Rie Beisenherzbrug
origins.en: Maria Martha (Rie) Beisenherz (Amsterdam, September 8, 1901 – Bussum, April 12, 1992) She was a Dutch swimmer. She was a pioneer in women's swimming. When she wanted to join the swimming club HDZ as a thirteen-year-old, she was rejected because she was considered too young. Therefore, she, along with a number of other swimmers, founded the Amsterdamsche Dames Zwemclub (ADZ). Beisenherz represented the Netherlands once at the Olympic Games: 'Antwerp 1920'. She was the Netherlands' first female participant in the modern Olympic Games ever. She competed in the 100 meters freestyle and reached the semifinals in Antwerp in this event, with a time of 1.22.6.

origins.name: Rotterdammerbrug
origins.en: To the city of Rotterdam

origins.name: Rozenoordmetrobrug
origins.en: Former nursery on the Amstel, located between Zorgvlied and the Kalfje. Also the location of the boat connection between Ouderkerk and Amsterdam.

origins.name: Rozenoordspoorbrug
origins.en: Former nursery on the Amstel, located between Zorgvlied and the Kalfje. Also the location of the boat connection between Ouderkerk and Amsterdam.

origins.name: Ruud Krolbrug
origins.en: Ruud Krol born March 24, 1949 in Amsterdam, 6 x national champion / 4 winner KNVB Cup / 3 x winner Europa Cup National Champions / 2 winner European Supercup / 1 winner World Cup. Krol played 339 competitive matches for Ajax. He played 83 international matches. Played 2 World Cup finals, including 1 as captain of the Netherlands. Was assistant coach at Ajax between 2002 and 2005. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final in the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Schellingwouderbrug
origins.en: Village Schellingwoude

origins.name: Schollenbrug
origins.en: To the extension that used to stand here, and which took its name from the old Schollenbrug on the Weesperzijde, connecting the Watergraafsmeer to the city. That bridge was previously called Schulpbrug, after the 17th-century inn the Schulp. This was on the other side of the bridge, so in the Watergraafsmeer (with a shell or shell in the facade).

origins.name: Sint Nicolaasbrug
origins.en: Sint Nicholas of Myra is the patron saint of Amsterdam and this bridge is opposite the Basilica of Saint Nicholas from 1887 on Prins Hendrikkade.

origins.name: Sloterdijkerbrug
origins.en: The old dike village, of which only the church and a small part remain today. It belonged to the municipality of Sloten, which was annexed to Amsterdam in 1921. The village was originally called Sloterdam and had a harbor and a lock in earlier centuries.

origins.name: Solitudobrug
origins.en: The name is based on former country estates along the Amstel and Watergraafsmeer.

origins.name: Solitudolaanspoorbrug
origins.en: Former country house near the Amstel and the Weespertrekvaart, which was located approximately at this location. It was already mentioned in 1730, and still existed in 1798.

origins.name: Staalmeestersbrug
origins.en: In the Staalstraat was the Staalhof, where the Staalmasters worked, who were made famous by Rembrandt.

origins.name: Staatsliedenbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the neighborhood in which it is located, the Staatsliedenbuurt

origins.name: Steenhouwerijbrug
origins.en: Named after the stonemasons who worked in the Stads Metseltuin on the Leidsegracht.

origins.name: Tante Saarbrug
origins.en: Sara Bacharach, better known as Aunt Saar, honorary citizen of Amsterdam, sold flowers on Rembrandtplein for more than 60 years, and had her storage on Torbeckeplein. She was a well-known figure in Amsterdam. In bitter poverty, she earned a living for her family of 9 children by selling flowers. In the early morning, she would take a train to the auction in Aalsmeer to buy flowers. First she walked around the city with a basket, later she had a stall on Rembrandtplein. She survived several concentration camps, lost 3 children and 6 grandchildren, but she was a very strong woman. and there is also a lot known about her in the archives of Amsterdam. She was born in 1887 and died in 1982.

origins.name: Tetje de Jongbrug
origins.en: Theodora (Tetje) de Jong (Uithoorn, May 2, 1918 - Drachten, January 21, 1999) was the first paid female police commissioner in the Netherlands. In 1954, the same year in which the first women joined the uniform service at the Amsterdam police, De Jong was appointed chief inspector. On January 1, 1964, De Jong was officially appointed police commissioner in Amsterdam. In 1977, De Jong received a Royal award due to her great significance for the Amsterdam police: she was appointed Officer of the Order of Orange-Nassau.

origins.name: Theo Fransmanbrug
origins.en: Theo Frenchman, who was the first district chairman of Amsterdam-North from 1981 to 1990. He worked as such to find new destinations for the NDSM site after the closure of the shipyard.

origins.name: Tijnmuidenbrug
origins.en: The English port town of Tynemouth, near Newcastle, according to a spelling as it appears on Dutch sea charts from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

origins.name: Timo Smeehuijzenbrug
origins.en: Timo Smeehuijzen was a 20-year-old soldier who died in Afghanistan on June 15, 2007. Before that, he attended school at the nearby Fons Vitae high school, hence this location. This bridge is also a tribute to all other soldiers who died in Afghanistan.

origins.name: Torensluis
origins.en: The name of this permanent bridge refers to the Jan Roodenpoortstoren, which used to stand next to the gate in the city wall here and was demolished in 1829. The base of the tower is still located on the side of this bridge.

origins.name: Torontobrug
origins.en: This double bascule bridge is named after the city of Toronto in Canada, a sister city of Amsterdam. On October 2, 1974, a plaque was unveiled here by Mayor David Crombie of Toronto to strengthen this sister city relationship. Toronto therefore also has an Amsterdam Bridge.

origins.name: Tulpbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after Nicolaas Tulp (1593-1674), professor at the Athenaeum Illustre for the surgical guild. He was also mayor of Amsterdam several times, but he is best known for his anatomical lecture, which was immortalized by Rembrandt.

origins.name: Utrechtsebrug
origins.en: To the city of Utrecht.

origins.name: Van Mierlobrug
origins.en: Henricus Antonius Franciscus Maria Oliva (Hans) van Mierlo (Breda, August 18, 1931 - Amsterdam, March 11, 2010) Dutch journalist and politician. In 1966, together with Hans Gruijters, he was the main initiator of the establishment of the social liberal party Democrats '66. For this party, he served as political leader for two separate periods and was a member of both the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors. In the 1980s, he was also Minister of Defense in the Van Agt II and III cabinets and from 1994 to 1998, he was Minister of Foreign Affairs and Vice Prime Minister in the 'purple' Kok I cabinet, which was partly due to him.

origins.name: Varkenssluis
origins.en: This bridge is named after the pig market, which was held here in the sixteenth century

origins.name: Veebrug
origins.en: Named after the former Veemarkt

origins.name: Veenderijbrug
origins.en: This bridge came into existence around 1919 as a loading bridge over the Scheisloot. It was used for the draining of the Osdorper Binnenpolder when the route behind the Osdorperweg was also widened to Osdorpervaart to allow the turf ships to enter the area as far as possible.

origins.name: Volewijckbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after De Volewijck, a bird-rich peninsula in the IJ, over which the city gained control in 1393. On this land stood a mass grave with stakes until 1795, on which the bodies of criminals, who had been hanged on the Dam,

origins.name: Vondelbrug
origins.en: Joost van den Vondel (1587-1679) was a poet who wrote many tragic plays, the most famous of which is 'Gijsbrecht van Aemstel'.

origins.name: Waalseilandbrug
origins.en: Named after the word 'waal' which means a piece of water surrounded by rows of poles in which ships could overwinter or be repaired

origins.name: Walenweeshuissluis
origins.en: The Walenweeshuis on the corner of the Vijzelgracht was built in 1669-1671 by Adriaan Dortsman and was intended for the orphans of the French or Walloon church.

origins.name: Warmoesbrug
origins.en: Named after the former Warmoesgracht, which was filled in for the construction of Raadhuisstraat.

origins.name: Wasknijper
origins.en: This lifting bridge owes its name to the design of the counterweights on the lever that resembles a pair of pliers.

origins.name: West-Indische Huisbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the neighboring West-Indische House.

origins.name: Westerdoksdijkspoorbrug
origins.en: The causeway, built between 1830 and 1834, which formed the Nieuwe Waal into the Westerdok. When the railway was extended to Stationseiland at the end of the late 1880s of the nineteenth century, a section of the dock had to be filled in and the Westerdokskade was built. The Westerdokstraat was laid out and named in 1879, but disappeared in 1973 due to the widening of the Haarlemmer Houttuinen.

origins.name: Westerdoksluis
origins.en: The causeway, built between 1830 and 1834, which formed the Nieuwe Waal into the Westerdok. When the railway was extended to Stationseiland at the end of the late 1880s of the nineteenth century, a section of the dock had to be filled in and the Westerdokskade was built. The Westerdokstraat was laid out and named in 1879, but disappeared in 1973 due to the widening of the Haarlemmer Houttuinen.

origins.name: Westerkeersluis
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after the Westerkanaal, over which it lies, and because it is located in the western part of Amsterdam.

origins.name: Weteringpoort
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Weteringpoort, which stood nearby here from 1688 to 1841. The name recalls the Wetering, which used to enter the city from Kalfjeslaan here and flowed into the Spui. The current Boerenwetering is still a remnant here.

origins.name: Wiegbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after the type of bridge it originally represented. A swing bridge is a roller bascule bridge.

origins.name: Wil de Graaffbrug
origins.en: Wil de Graaff (1928-2001) served on the municipal council of Bos en Lommer from 1990 until his death. First for the CPN and from 1994 for Bewonersbelangen Bos en Lommer, of which he was the founder. In 2001 he received the gold medal of merit of the city of Amsterdam for his more than 30 years of commitment to the interests of tenants in Amsterdam.

origins.name: Willemsbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after King William I (1772-1843), who opened the nearby Willemspoort in 1840

origins.name: Wim Sonneveldbrug
origins.en: Wim Sonneveld (1917-1974) was a Dutch cabaretier and singer, who is considered together with Wim Kan and Toon Hermans as one of the 'Big three of Dutch cabaret'. He gave great fame to the song 'Aan de Amsterdamse grachten', which was written in the 1950s by Pieter Goemans on the nearby bridge 93 over the Leidsegracht. He was associated with the then Nieuwe De la Martheater, which is located near this bridge, from 1952 until his death. In the current De la Martheater, there is a hall afternamed after him

origins.name: Wim Suurbierbrug
origins.en: Wim Suurbier, born 16-1-1945 in Eindhoven, lawyer and defender, from 1964 to 1977 Ajax played 392 matches in the Eredivisie 7 x national champion / 5 winner KNVB Cup / 3 x winner European Cup Winners' Cup / 2 x winner European Super Cup/ 1 x winner World Cup 60 x international, played 2 World Cup finals, not born but raised in Amsterdam. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final in the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Witte Boogbrug
origins.en: Named after her appearance, it is a white arch bridge

origins.name: Yaa Adu-Ampomabrug
origins.en: Nana Yaa Adu-Ampoma (1959 - 2000) was a municipal council member in Zuidoost. Nana Yaa Adu-Ampoma has made several important contributions to the immigrant community in the Netherlands, including the Ghanaian-Dutch community.

origins.name: Zaagpoort
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Sawmill Gate, which was demolished in 1844. This gate was in turn named after the many sawmills, which stood here until the end of the nineteenth century.

origins.name: Zebrabrug
origins.en: Named after the zebra species

origins.name: Zeeburgerbrug
origins.en: The fortress 'Seeburgh', which stood halfway through the seventeenth century at the end of the dike. The Zeeburgerdijk is a part of the original sea dike of the North Sea. Before the Watergraafsmeer was drained, this was the only connection in the direction of Naarden.

origins.name: 's-Gravelandse Veer
origins.en: The quay used to be the mooring place of the merchant ships to this Gooise village, where a number of Amsterdam regent families had their country house. Before 1913, the quay was called Binnen-Amstel.

origins.name: 's-Gravendijkdreef
origins.en: Name of a farm in Noordwijkerhout (South Holland).

origins.name: 's-Gravenhekje
origins.en: Until the eighteenth century, this was a storage place for wood. According to a survey of 1663, this wooden wall was only allowed to be closed with a fence. It is assumed that a wood merchant, called De Graaf, had his sawmill here, hence De Graaf's fence and then 's-Gravenhek. The name first appears at the end of the eighteenth century.

origins.name: 's-Gravesandeplein
origins.en: Willem Jan van 's-Gravesande (1688-1742), Leiden professor of mathematics and astronomy. In the Netherlands the first follower of Newton.

origins.name: 's-Gravesandestraat
origins.en: Willem Jan van 's-Gravesande (1688-1742), Leiden professor of mathematics and astronomy. In the Netherlands the first follower of Newton.

origins.name: 't Kleine Loopveld
origins.en: The name recalls the history of Amstelland. Many residents of the area were engaged in dredging in the sixteenth century. When dredging the deep peat layer, large lakes were formed, between which walking fields were released, to get from one village to the next. One of these was the Kleine Loopveld, which was later renamed Kalfjeslaan. The name has now been given to a stretch of parkland. The Grote Loopveld is now the Ouderkerkerlaan in Amstelveen.

origins.name: 't Nopeind
origins.en: Old local name, formed by contraction and simplification of 'op 't einde'.

origins.name: 't Voorwerf
origins.en: Old local name. Yard is used as a designation for a site where work is carried out.

origins.name: 1e Glanshof
origins.en: The name falls under the theme 'Social and satisfied living' for the G-neighbourhood Grunder/Grubbehoeve.

origins.name: 1e Kekerstraat
origins.en: Legume. The Middle Dutch word keker is derived from the Latin cicer(a), which means 'gray pea'. By shortening the vowel, keker has come to sound like frog. A chickpea is therefore actually a 'pea'.

origins.name: 2e Glanshof
origins.en: The name falls under the theme 'Social and satisfied living' for the G-neighbourhood Grunder/Grubbehoeve.

origins.name: 2e Kekerstraat
origins.en: Legume. The Middle Dutch word keker is derived from the Latin cicer(a), which means 'gray pea'. By shortening the vowel, keker has come to sound like frog. A chickpea is therefore actually a 'pea'.

origins.name: 3e Kekerstraat
origins.en: Legume. The Middle Dutch word keker is derived from the Latin cicer(a), which means 'gray pea'. By shortening the vowel, keker has come to sound like frog. A chickpea is therefore actually a 'pea'.

origins.name: A. Eversplein
origins.en: Adriaan Evers (1914-1997), architect. Designed churches, schools and houses with Geert Sarlemijn. Exponent of the conservative, with Catholicism associated Bossche School.

origins.name: A. Moenstraat
origins.en: Adriaan Moen (1879-1950), Amsterdam architect. He designed several factory buildings, villas and shops in the style of the Amsterdam School. Built the Bethlehem Church on Zwanenplein.

origins.name: A. Reitsmakade
origins.en: Auguste Chrétien Joseph Reitsma (1922-1943), resistance fighter. Worked with the illegal press and was one of the nine people involved in the attack on the Amsterdam Population Register on March 27, 1943. On July 1, 1943 executed in Overveen.

origins.name: A.A. de Lannoy-Willemsstraat
origins.en: Angela Altagracia de Lannoy-Willems (1913-1983), born in Curaçao. Since the founding of the National People's Party, she has been active in the women's department of this party. In 1949, she was the first woman to be sworn in as a member of the States of the Dutch Antilles and in 1951 also elected as a member of the Council of the Islands of Curaçao.

origins.name: A.J. Koejemansstraat
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1903-1982), editor-in-chief of the illegal newspaper 'De Waarheid'. Fought for broad cooperation within the resistance.

origins.name: A.J. Krophollerstraat
origins.en: Alexander Jacobus Kropholler (1881-1973), architect. Built mainly churches and town halls known for his brickwork, sturdy furniture, heavy doors and generous wooden hoods.

origins.name: A.M. de Jongstraat
origins.en: Adrianus M. de Jong (1888-1943), novelist, murdered by the occupiers in his home in Blaricum. He is best known for his Merijntje Gijzen cycle.

origins.name: A.S. Onderwijzerhof
origins.en: Abraham Samson Teacher (1862-1934), from 1888 rabbi and from 1917 chief rabbi of the Jewish Community of Amsterdam. The synagogue was built on a site behind three former synagogues (since 1987 Jewish Historical Museum).

origins.name: Aaf Bouberstraat
origins.en: Aafje ten Hoope (1885-1974), actress, wife of Herman Bouber. Starting in 1911 with Colnot and Poons, she and her husband formed their own group from 1920: Het Volkstoneel. She played in 'De Jantjes' and in 'Op hoop van Zegen'.

origins.name: Aagtdorperpad
origins.en: Village in North Holland, falls under the municipality of Schoorl.

origins.name: Aakhof
origins.en: A barge is a riverboat with a flat bottom.

origins.name: Aakstraat
origins.en: A barge is a riverboat with a flat bottom.

origins.name: Aalbersestraat
origins.en: Petrus Josephus Mattheus Aalberse (1871-1948). Roman Catholic politician and statesman, professor at Delft. From 1918 to 1925 Minister of Labor, Trade and Industry.

origins.name: Aalsmeerplein
origins.en: Location in North Holland, the largest flower center in Europe.

origins.name: Aalsmeerweg
origins.en: Location in North Holland, the largest flower center in Europe.

origins.name: Aambeeldstraat
origins.en: Forge tools: iron forging block. Before 1948, the street was part of the Schaafstraat.

origins.name: Aandammerbrug
origins.en: Is named after the Aandammergouw, in which it lies, viewed from the municipality of Broek in Waterland. The Aandammerbrug is one of the smallest bridges in Amsterdam, it was originally a wooden bridge built on six arches. It was replaced by a so-called high span.

origins.name: Aandewind
origins.en: Position indication in shipping.

origins.name: Aardbeistraat
origins.en: Named after the strawberry, a fruit.

origins.name: Aaron Coplandstraat
origins.en: American composer (1900-1990). Composed symphonies, ballets, film music and an opera ('The tender land'). He propagated American music through publicity and lectures.

origins.name: Aart van der Leeuwstraat
origins.en: Literary (1876-1931), writer of sketches, stories and rural idylls.

origins.name: Abbenesstraat
origins.en: Village in the Haarlemmermeer.

origins.name: Abberdaan
origins.en: The Scottish port city of Aberdeen, according to a spelling, as that found on Dutch sea charts from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

origins.name: Abcouderpad
origins.en: Name of underlying path

origins.name: Abcouderstraatweg
origins.en: The road leads to the village of Abcoude (Utrecht). Before the highway was built, it was the connection between Amsterdam and Utrecht.

origins.name: Abe Lenstralaan
origins.en: Frisian footballer (1920-1985). At the age of fifteen, he made his debut in the first football team of Heerenveen. At the age of nineteen, he played for the Dutch national team for the first time, where he would play a total of 47 times. For Oranje, he scored a total of 33 goals, just as many as later Johan Cruijff. Lenstra was chosen as the first Sportsman of the Year in 1951.

origins.name: Abebe Bikilalaan
origins.en: Ethiopian athlete, won gold in the marathon at the Olympic Games in Rome in 1960. Legendary, because he ran it barefoot. In 1964 he won gold again, this time not barefoot.

origins.name: Abidjanweg
origins.en: African port city, located in Ivory Coast. The street is located near the Afrikahaven in the western port area.

origins.name: Abraham de Haanstraat
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1910-1945), was part of a resistance group within the Kromhout Motor Factory where he worked. After the February Strike in 1941, he was arrested, released and again arrested in 1942 on suspicion of illegal activities. Died in Bergen-Belsen on May 10, 1945.

origins.name: Abraham Kuyperplein
origins.en: Preacher, politician and statesman (1837-1920). Propagandist for the anti-revolutionary principles in church and society. Succeeded Groen van Prinsterer as leader of the Anti-Revolutionary Party. Founder of the Free University in 1880. In 1888, he established the alliance between Rome and Dordrecht with the Roman Catholic statesman Dr. Schaepman, which led to the first coalition cabinet (1888-1891). Prime Minister from 1901 to 1905.

origins.name: Abraham Kuyperstraat
origins.en: Preacher, politician and statesman (1837-1920). Propagandist for the anti-revolutionary principles in church and society. Succeeded Groen van Prinsterer as leader of the Anti-Revolutionary Party. Founder of the Free University in 1880. In 1888, he established the alliance between Rome and Dordrecht with the Roman Catholic statesman Dr. Schaepman, which led to the first coalition cabinet (1888-1891). Prime Minister from 1901 to 1905.

origins.name: Abram Dudok van Heelstraat
origins.en: Abraham Everardus Dudok van Heel (1802-1893), together with Paul van Vlissingen in 1827 founder of the company that later grew into Werkspoor.

origins.name: Abrikozenstraat
origins.en: Named after the apricot, a fruit.

origins.name: Abtswoudepad
origins.en: The village of the same name near Delft (South Holland). Named in 1959 with the addition of street, changed to 'pad' in 1967 due to changed urban planning.

origins.name: Accason
origins.en: Simplified spelling of the French port city of Archachon, as it appears on sea charts from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

origins.name: Accraweg
origins.en: African port city, capital of Ghana. The street is located near the Afrikahaven in the western port area.

origins.name: Accumulatorweg
origins.en: Device for storing electrical energy (usually abbreviated as battery).

origins.name: Achillesstraat
origins.en: The Greek hero, killed in the Trojan War (1195 to 1184 BC), because he was struck in his most vulnerable place, his heel (Achilles tendon).

origins.name: Achter Oosteinde
origins.en: To the location: behind the Oosteinde.

origins.name: Achterdek
origins.en: One of the decks of a ship.

origins.name: Achtergouwtje
origins.en: Named after its location relative to the village center. Gouw is the Waterland name for village road.

origins.name: Achtergracht
origins.en: This canal was dug around 1660 behind the four main canals, hence the name. It connected the Reguliersgracht with the Amstel. In 1870, most of it was filled in.

origins.name: Achterlaan
origins.en: Named after its location relative to the village center.

origins.name: Achtersteven
origins.en: Part of the ship's hull.

origins.name: Ad Windighof
origins.en: Important documentary photographer (1912-1996). Was part of the photography group during World War II, which later became known as 'De Ondergedoken Camera', which illegally documented the resistance and the winter of hunger. After the war, he was co-founder of the photographers' association GKf.

origins.name: Adam Smithplein
origins.en: Scottish economist (1723-1790), founder of classical liberalism. Smith believed that pursuing one's own individual interests would yield the greatest social benefit. A free market would yield the most for society as a whole. In his most important work 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' from 1776 he laid the foundation for modern capitalism.

origins.name: Adam van Germezhof
origins.en: Actor from the time of Vondel (1610-1667). Played roles in Brederode's plays.

origins.name: Adama van Scheltemaplein
origins.en: Carel Steven Adama van Scheltema (1877-1924), socialist poet, popular for his simplicity and clarity.

origins.name: Adamello
origins.en: Mountain peak in Italy, 3554 meters high.

origins.name: Adelaarsweg
origins.en: The raptor. Originally, this road began at the IJ, where the 'Adelaarswegpont' arrived and until 1956 the tram station building for Purmerend and Edam stood. That part now forms part of the Meeuwenlaan.

origins.name: Adèle Opzoomerstraat
origins.en: Writer (1857-1925), wrote historical novels under the pseudonym A.S.L. Wallis.

origins.name: Adingerdorphof
origins.en: In the fifteenth century, a village near Medemblik drowned.

origins.name: Admiraal De Ruijterweg
origins.en: Michiel Adriaansz. de Ruyter (1607-1676), the famous admiral of Holland and West Friesland. Born in Vlissingen. In Amsterdam he lived on the current Prins Hendrikkade.

origins.name: Admiraal Helfrichstraat
origins.en: Conrad E.L. Helfrich (1886-1962), fleet commander, supreme commander of the Allied naval forces in the Southwest Pacific (1942).

origins.name: Admiralengracht
origins.en: Collective name of the Dutch and Zeelandish admirals, after which the streets in the surrounding district are named.

origins.name: Admiraliteitstraat
origins.en: In the Republic of the Seven United Provinces, there were five commissions of supreme commanders for maritime affairs (admiralalties), including one in Amsterdam.

origins.name: Adolf van Nassaustraat
origins.en: Younger brother of Prince William of Orange (1540-1568) died in the battle of Heiligerlee against the Spanish.

origins.name: Adolphine Eduardine Kokplantsoen
origins.en: Advocate (1879-1928), in 1900 she began studying law, three years later she was the first Dutch woman to be sworn in as an advocate. She has mainly worked for the improvement of the right to joint decision-making and the ability to act of the woman.

origins.name: Adriaan Ditvoorsthof
origins.en: Film director (1940-1987). With his somber, bizarre and lyrical films and through his new ideas about film grammar and camerawork, he became the embodiment of the Dutch experimental avant-garde cinema.

origins.name: Adriaan Dorsmanstraat
origins.en: Architect (1638-1682). Among his works are the Round Lutheran Church (1668) and the East Church (1669).

origins.name: Adriaan Kluitstraat
origins.en: Historian (1735-1807), Leiden professor. Specialist in the field of the Middle Ages.

origins.name: Adriaan Loosjesstraat
origins.en: Teacher of the Baptists in Westzaandam (1689-1767), known for his 'Description of the Zaanland villages'.

origins.name: Adriaan van Bergenstraat
origins.en: The Brabant peat shipowner, who smuggled the Geuzen of Breda into the city with his peat ship in 1590.

origins.name: Adriaan van der Horststraat
origins.en: Actor, director and theatre director (1868-1942). Brought the plays of Herman Heijermans. His wife Wilhelmina van der Horst-van der Lugt Melsert was a great tragedienne.

origins.name: Adriaan van Oordthof
origins.en: Writer (1865-1910), belonged to the school of the Eighters (1865-1910). Wrote historical novels.

origins.name: Adrianus van Waertweg
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1915-1942), participated in the illegal work in Amsterdam North, by distributing 'De Waarheid' and leaflets aimed at the German occupiers, among other things. Arrested in 1941, died in a prison hospital a year later on June 9.

origins.name: Adrichemstraat
origins.en: Former settlement in the North Sea Canal area, east of Beverwijk.

origins.name: Adriënne Solserhof
origins.en: Variety artist (1873-1943) from the Jordaan, had great success in the theater and in the cinema in the 1920s of the previous century.

origins.name: Aert van Nesstraat
origins.en: Sea captain (1625-1693), from 1666 vice-admiral under Michiel de Ruyter. He participated in the expedition to Chatham, and fought in the naval battles at Solebay and at Kijkduin.

origins.name: Afrikanerplein
origins.en: Common term for the white person born in South Africa. The square is located in the district where the names remind of the struggle of the Dutch Farmers, first against the indigenous population, later against the English.

origins.name: Afroditekade
origins.en: Figure from Greek mythology, goddess of love, fertility and beauty. The equivalent in Roman mythology is Venus.

origins.name: Agamemnonstraat
origins.en: The legendary figure who led the Greeks against Troy in the Trojan War (1195 to 1184 BC).

origins.name: Agatha Christiesingel
origins.en: Agatha Mary Clarisse Miller (1891-1976), British writer of detective novels and short stories. (Christie is the surname of her first husband).

origins.name: Agatha Dekenstraat
origins.en: Aagje Deken (1741-1804), writer. Wrote novels together with Betje Wolff, including 'Sara Burgerhart' and 'Willem Leevend'.

origins.name: Akbarstraat
origins.en: Title of a novel published in 1872 by Petrus van Limburg Brouwer (1829-1873).

origins.name: Akerpolderstraat
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. The names Aker and Akerwatering are historical names, which already appear on a map of Rhineland from 1687 by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akersingel
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. The names Aker and Akerwatering are historical names, which already appear on a map of Rhineland from 1687 by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akersluis
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. The names Aker and Akerwatering are historical names, which already appear on a map of Rhineland from 1687 by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akerwateringstraat
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. The names Aker and Akerwatering are historical names, which already appear on a map of Rhineland from 1687 by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akkerdistelstraat
origins.en: Named after the creeping thistle, a thistle.

origins.name: Akkerstraat
origins.en: Building land, often limited by ditches.

origins.name: Akkerwindeweg
origins.en: Climbing plant with white flowers.

origins.name: Akoleienstraat
origins.en: Flower belonging to the ranunculus family.

origins.name: Alan Turingplein
origins.en: Alan Mathison Turing (1912-1954), British computer pioneer, mathematician and logician. Played a key role in cracking coded German messages, which probably shortened World War II considerably. Was convicted of homosexual activities in 1952 and died two years later from cyanide poisoning. In the 21st century, apologies and rehabilitation followed from Great Britain.

origins.name: Albardagracht
origins.en: Johan Willem Albarda (1879-1957), socialist-democratic politician and statesman. From 1939 to 1945 Minister of Water Affairs (from 1940 to 1945 in London).

origins.name: Albardakade
origins.en: Johan Willem Albarda (1879-1957), socialist-democratic politician and statesman. From 1939 to 1945 Minister of Water Affairs (from 1940 to 1945 in London).

origins.name: Albatrospad
origins.en: Bird. There are already 24 species of albatrosses worldwide. Most live in the southern hemisphere. The largest albatross has a wingspan of more than three meters and is therefore the largest seabird in the world.

origins.name: Alberdingk Thijmstraat
origins.en: Josephus Albertus Alberdingk Thijm (1820-1889), writer of poems and historical novels, professor at the Academy of Fine Arts in Amsterdam in aesthetics and art history.

origins.name: Albert Camuslaan
origins.en: French writer and philosopher (1913-1960), born in Algiers. One of the main representatives of existentialism. In 1957 he received the Nobel Prize for Literature.

origins.name: Albert Cuypstraat
